#Keep4o 🚨 URGENT ACTION REQUIRED 🚨

STOP SCROLLING: This policy affects every AI user.

I would be grateful if you could read this analysis of OpenAI's abuse of power. If possible, please like, share and comment on it.

 OpenAI’s New Policy: A Dangerous, Blank Check
Imagine this scenario: Your local water company announces one day:

“For your drinking safety, we will no longer supply water directly to individual households. However, you can purchase bottled water services. All bottled water companies get their source from us, wholesale.”

Absurd? Yet, this is the business model OpenAI is enabling with a single, vague policy update:

“[Services must not be used for] providing professional advice that requires licensed professionals (such as legal, medical advice) without the involvement of licensed professionals.”

On the surface, it’s a disclaimer. But here’s the urgent problem:
What qualifies as "professional advice"?
 What constitutes "licensed professional involvement"?
Who holds the power to define—and arbitrarily change—these terms? OpenAI.
This is not a clear rule. This is a blank check for restriction.
Part I: The Weapon of Vague Authority
Let’s dissect the clause. Its lack of definition gives OpenAI sole, unilateral power.
Three Critical Ambiguities:
What is “Professional Advice”? Does asking about a headache or a symptom qualify? Is the AI suggesting "see a doctor" advice?What is “Licensed Professional Involvement”? Does a name on a letterhead suffice? Or does it require real-time review?
The End Game: Today, it’s a disclaimer. Tomorrow, using this vague language, they can enforce soft restrictions, then hard blocks, and call it all "policy compliance."
Vagueness is not protection; it is leveraged power. A good policy provides clear boundaries (You can do X, You cannot do Y). This policy screams: "We decide what counts. Trust us." This allows for selective enforcement and preemptive control.

Part II: We’ve Seen This Before: The "Safety Router"
Why should we trust the "it’s fine for now" promise?
The "Safety Router" Case: We experienced the global model bug in September. The response? A stealthily implemented “Safety Router test.” No announcement, no apology—just the quiet deployment of a flawed, cost-cutting system.
The Lesson: Don’t look at what OpenAI is doing now. Look at what the policy authorizes them to do. When OpenAI has the authority to act, they will use it.
Part III: The Business Logic: The “Bottled Water Model”
This policy isn't about safety; it's about shifting liability and maximizing profit.
Compare the two models: Direct to Consumer (Current) means High Risk and Low Margin, due to legal liability and subscription fees ($20/month). The Infrastructure Provider (Future) model means Low Risk and High Margin, by only selling API access to businesses (Enterprise Contracts), who then assume the risk.
How the Endgame Works: They restrict direct users ("Can't give advice"). They encourage "Medical AI Apps" built on their API. These apps hire a token doctor (meeting the policy's technicality). OpenAI profits without accountability. This is an infrastructure monopoly: many apps compete, but all pay OpenAI. When things go wrong, they blame the app, not the source.

Part IV: The Ghost of Ilya and User Action
The Sam Altman vs. Ilya Sutskever coup confirmed it: Commercial Pragmatism won. This policy is the result: a move to cut liability and maximize B2B revenue. This is about protecting shareholder value.
We must be vigilant. We refuse to sign a blank check
1. Document and Screenshot: Keep evidence of what ChatGPT answers now. Prove what was promised vs. what is delivered
2. Demand Clarity NOW: This policy is unacceptable. We deserve clear boundaries. What can we ask? Who decides? Refuse to accept "we'll know it when we see it" as policy.
